title: Neoplasia
summary: How normal cells become cancer and how cancer behaves.

lessons.title: Benign vs Malignant Tumors

levels.kid:
Normally, your cells grow and divide only when your body needs new ones, like a garden where plants grow just the right amount.

Sometimes cells stop listening and keep growing when they should not. That makes a lump called a **tumor**.

Some tumors are **benign**. They grow slowly, stay in one place, and have a neat edge, like a ball. They are usually not dangerous, although some still need to be taken out.

Other tumors are **malignant**. That is **cancer**. They grow fast, push into nearby parts like weeds, and can send cells traveling to faraway places in the body.

Doctors look at tumor cells under a microscope to tell which kind it is.
levels.hs:
**Neoplasia** means 'new growth': an abnormal mass of cells growing beyond normal control, continuing even after the trigger is gone. The mass is a **neoplasm** or **tumor**.

Tumors are either **benign** or **malignant**:
- **Benign** tumors grow slowly, are usually surrounded by a capsule, push nearby tissue aside without invading it, look similar to normal cells (**well differentiated**), and **never spread** to distant sites.
- **Malignant** tumors (**cancers**) often grow faster, **invade** surrounding tissue, can look very abnormal, and can **metastasize**: spread to distant organs through blood or lymph.

Metastasis is the single most reliable sign of malignancy, and it causes most cancer deaths.

**Naming tumors**:
- Benign tumors usually end in **-oma**: lipoma (fat), adenoma (gland), fibroma (fibrous tissue).
- Malignant tumors of epithelial cells are **carcinomas** (most common: lung, breast, colon, prostate).
- Malignant tumors of connective tissue like bone or muscle are **sarcomas** (osteosarcoma).
- Blood cancers are **leukemias** and **lymphomas**.
- Some names break the rules: **melanoma**, **lymphoma** and **glioblastoma** are malignant despite ending in -oma.

Brain tumors are special: even a benign tumor can be deadly because the skull is a closed box, and location matters as much as behavior.
levels.college:
**Features distinguishing benign from malignant**:
- **Differentiation and anaplasia**: differentiation is how closely tumor cells resemble normal cells. **Anaplasia** (lack of differentiation) is a hallmark of malignancy: pleomorphism (variation in size and shape), hyperchromatic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, abundant and atypical mitoses, tumor giant cells, and loss of polarity.
- **Rate of growth**: generally faster in malignancy, but variable.
- **Local invasion**: the most reliable feature after metastasis; benign tumors are often encapsulated.
- **Metastasis**: unequivocal marker of malignancy (with rare exceptions: basal cell carcinoma and most primary brain tumors invade locally but rarely metastasize outside the CNS).

**Pathways of spread**:
- **Seeding of body cavities** (ovarian cancer across the peritoneum; CSF dissemination of medulloblastoma, 'drop metastases').
- **Lymphatic spread**, typical of carcinomas; sentinel lymph node biopsy samples the first draining node.
- **Hematogenous spread**, typical of sarcomas (also renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma invading veins). Liver and lungs are common sites.

**Dysplasia**: disordered growth with atypia, often preceding cancer. When it involves the full thickness of an epithelium without breaching the basement membrane, it is **carcinoma in situ**; breach of the basement membrane defines **invasive carcinoma**.

**Nomenclature traps**: hamartoma (disorganized but mature tissue native to the site, such as pulmonary hamartoma) and choristoma (normal tissue in an abnormal location, such as pancreatic rest in the stomach) are not true neoplasms. Teratomas contain tissues from multiple germ layers; mature teratomas are usually benign, immature ones can be malignant. Mixed tumors (pleomorphic adenoma of the salivary gland) contain divergent differentiation from one clone.

**Epidemiology**: age is the strongest risk factor; environmental factors include tobacco, alcohol, obesity, infections (HPV, hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, EBV), UV and ionizing radiation.
levels.phd:
Tumors are **clonal**, arising from a single cell that acquired advantageous genetic and epigenetic changes, as shown historically by X-chromosome inactivation patterns (G6PD isoforms in leiomyomas) and now by shared mutations across tumor cells. But clonal origin evolves into **intratumoral heterogeneity**: multi-region sequencing of renal cell carcinomas revealed that a single biopsy captures only part of a branching phylogeny, with driver mutations differing between regions. Tumors evolve by Darwinian selection, and therapy is a selective pressure that enriches resistant subclones.

The benign-malignant distinction is biological, not merely morphological. Benign tumors usually have few driver alterations (for example, a single pathway activation such as BRAF V600E in many benign nevi, which then enter oncogene-induced senescence), whereas carcinomas accumulate multiple hits. The **adenoma-carcinoma sequence** in colon cancer (APC loss, KRAS activation, TP53 loss, with other changes) is the classic model, though alternative routes exist: serrated polyps with BRAF mutation and CpG island methylation, and mismatch repair deficiency producing hypermutated tumors.

**Metastasis** is inefficient: millions of tumor cells can enter the circulation daily, but very few form metastases. The 'seed and soil' hypothesis (Paget, 1889) proposed organ-specific compatibility; modern work adds **premetastatic niches** prepared by tumor-secreted exosomes and factors, and the observation that dissemination can occur early, with disseminated cells remaining **dormant** for years before relapse (classic in breast cancer and melanoma).

The World Health Organization classification of CNS tumors (fifth edition, 2021) shows how molecular features now redefine tumor identity: diffuse gliomas are classified by IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion status, and an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic glioma with certain molecular features (TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or chromosome 7 gain with chromosome 10 loss) is classified as glioblastoma even when it looks lower grade under the microscope. Morphology is no longer the whole story.
levels.expert:
**Never call a mass benign without tissue**, unless imaging is truly pathognomonic. Biopsy approach matters: a sarcoma biopsy should be placed along the future resection line, because the tract can seed tumor; a poorly planned biopsy can cost a limb. Discuss with the treating surgeon first.

**Brain tumors upend the benign/malignant rule**. A meningioma is usually WHO grade 1, slow growing and curable by complete resection, yet a large skull-base meningioma encasing arteries and cranial nerves can be impossible to remove fully without disability. Neurosurgeons describe resection with the **Simpson grade**, and decide between observation, surgery and radiosurgery based on size, growth, symptoms and location. Conversely, glioblastoma is diffusely infiltrative: tumor cells extend well beyond the enhancing margin seen on MRI, so 'gross total resection' means removing the enhancing tumor, not every cell. Fluorescence guidance (5-aminolevulinic acid makes tumor glow pink under blue light) and intraoperative mapping help maximize safe resection.

**Metastases are the most common brain tumors in adults**: lung, breast, melanoma, kidney and colon are frequent sources. A new ring-enhancing lesion in an adult with a cancer history is metastasis until proven otherwise, but abscess and primary tumor remain on the differential. Single accessible metastases may be resected, often followed by stereotactic radiosurgery to the cavity; multiple small ones are often treated with radiosurgery alone.

**Reading a pathology report**: look for tumor type, grade, margins (positive or negative, and distance), lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, lymph node status, and molecular markers. Each changes treatment.

**Talk to patients carefully**: 'benign' brain tumor can still mean seizures, surgery and lifelong follow-up, and 'cancer' covers diseases ranging from curable to rapidly fatal. Precision in words prevents both false reassurance and needless fear.

keyPoints: Neoplasm: autonomous abnormal growth that persists after the stimulus
Benign: slow, encapsulated, well differentiated, no metastasis
Malignant: invasion, anaplasia, metastasis (the definitive sign)
Carcinoma = epithelial malignancy; sarcoma = connective tissue malignancy
Carcinomas spread mainly by lymphatics; sarcomas mainly by blood
In the brain, location can make a benign tumor deadly

examples.tr: Benign tumor of fat: soft, movable, encapsulated.
Malignant tumor of bone; spreads by blood, often to lung.
Usually benign but can compress the brain and need surgery.

lessons.title: Oncogenes and Tumor Suppressor Genes

levels.kid:
Inside every cell is an instruction book called **DNA**. It tells the cell when to grow and when to stop.

Think of a car. Some genes are like the **gas pedal**: they tell the cell to grow. Other genes are like the **brakes**: they tell the cell to stop.

Cancer can start when the gas pedal gets stuck down. Doctors call a stuck gas pedal gene an **oncogene**.

Cancer can also start when the brakes break. Brake genes are called **tumor suppressor genes**.

Usually a cell needs several broken parts before it becomes cancer. That is one reason most cancers happen in older people: it takes time to break that many parts.
levels.hs:
Cancer is a disease of **genes**. Mutations, changes in DNA, alter proteins that control cell growth, division and death. Two major classes of genes matter:

**Proto-oncogenes** normally promote growth, for example by sending 'divide now' signals. When mutated or overactive, they become **oncogenes**, like a gas pedal stuck down. Only **one** copy needs to be changed for the effect (a gain of function, dominant). Examples: **RAS** (mutated in many pancreatic, colon and lung cancers), **HER2** (overactive in some breast cancers), **MYC**.

**Tumor suppressor genes** normally restrain growth or repair DNA, like brakes. Usually **both** copies must be lost before the cell loses control (a loss of function, recessive at the cell level). Examples:
- **TP53**, 'the guardian of the genome', which stops damaged cells from dividing or tells them to die. It is mutated in about half of all cancers.
- **RB**, which controls the checkpoint before DNA copying.
- **BRCA1 and BRCA2**, which repair DNA breaks; inherited mutations raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.

A third group, **DNA repair genes**, fixes mistakes. When they fail, mutations pile up faster.

Mutations can be **inherited** (present in every cell from birth, explaining family cancer syndromes) or **acquired** during life from copying errors, smoking, UV light and radiation. Most cancers come from acquired mutations.
levels.college:
**Mechanisms of oncogene activation**:
- **Point mutations**: KRAS (codon 12), keeping RAS locked in its GTP-bound active state by impairing GTPase activity; BRAF V600E in melanoma.
- **Gene amplification**: HER2 (ERBB2) in breast cancer, N-MYC in neuroblastoma, EGFR in glioblastoma.
- **Chromosomal translocations**: BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia (the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)), producing a constitutively active tyrosine kinase; MYC with immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer in Burkitt lymphoma, t(8;14); BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, t(14;18), blocking apoptosis.

Oncogene products include growth factors, receptors (EGFR, HER2, RET, KIT), signal transducers (RAS, BRAF, ABL), transcription factors (MYC) and cell cycle regulators (cyclin D, CDK4).

**Knudson's two-hit hypothesis**, from retinoblastoma: in hereditary cases, one RB mutation is inherited (first hit in every cell), so a single somatic hit causes tumor, explaining early, bilateral, multifocal tumors. Sporadic cases require two somatic hits in the same cell, so they are later and unilateral. **Loss of heterozygosity** is the usual second hit.

**RB** binds E2F transcription factors; phosphorylation by cyclin D-CDK4/6 releases E2F, pushing the cell past the G1/S checkpoint. HPV E7 inactivates RB; HPV E6 targets p53 for degradation.

**TP53** responds to DNA damage (via ATM/ATR kinases) by inducing p21 (cell-cycle arrest), DNA repair genes, or apoptosis (BAX, PUMA). MDM2 normally degrades p53. Germline TP53 mutations cause **Li-Fraumeni syndrome** (sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma, leukemia).

**Other suppressors**: APC (Wnt pathway, familial adenomatous polyposis), NF1 (a RAS GTPase-activating protein; neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (merlin; vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas), VHL (hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma), PTEN (PI3K pathway).

**DNA repair defects**: mismatch repair genes in Lynch syndrome; BRCA in homologous recombination.
levels.phd:
The oncogene/tumor suppressor framework has been refined in several directions.

**Haploinsufficiency and dosage**: Knudson's strict two-hit model does not always hold. Some tumor suppressors act when only one copy is lost (haploinsufficiency), and some, like PTEN, show graded dosage effects in which partial loss promotes tumors in a dose-dependent way. Mutant p53 proteins can also act as **dominant negatives** and even gain new oncogenic functions, so TP53 missense mutations differ biologically from deletions.

**Oncogene addiction**: tumors driven by a single dominant oncogene can become dependent on it, so inhibiting it causes dramatic regression: imatinib in BCR-ABL leukemia transformed chronic myeloid leukemia from a fatal disease into a manageable condition with near-normal life expectancy for many patients. **Synthetic lethality** exploits the opposite: tumors lacking BRCA function depend on alternative repair, so PARP inhibitors selectively kill them.

**Long-undruggable targets fall**: KRAS was considered undruggable for decades until covalent inhibitors targeting the G12C mutant (sotorasib, adagrasib) exploited a cysteine pocket in the inactive state; inhibitors of other variants and pan-RAS approaches are in development. Resistance emerges quickly through adaptive feedback and new mutations.

**Epigenetic tumor suppression**: silencing by promoter hypermethylation (MLH1 in sporadic microsatellite-unstable colon cancer; MGMT in glioblastoma) can substitute for a genetic hit. **Oncometabolites** blur the line further: mutant IDH1/2 produces 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases, creating a hypermethylated phenotype (G-CIMP) in gliomas. IDH inhibitors such as vorasidenib extended progression-free survival in low-grade IDH-mutant glioma (INDIGO trial, 2023).

**Histone mutations** define pediatric tumors: H3 K27M in diffuse midline glioma, where a single amino acid change inhibits PRC2 globally, a striking example of an 'oncohistone'.

Genomic catalogs show that cancers differ widely in mutation burden, from very few in pediatric tumors to hundreds per megabase in mismatch repair-deficient or UV-driven cancers.
levels.expert:
Molecular oncology is now routine clinical practice, and neurosurgeons operate on tumors whose identity is defined by genes.

**Glioma workup**: the tissue you remove goes for IDH mutation status, 1p/19q codeletion (defines oligodendroglioma), ATRX, TP53, MGMT promoter methylation, CDKN2A/B deletion (an adverse marker in IDH-mutant astrocytomas), and often a DNA methylation profile. **MGMT methylation** predicts benefit from temozolomide chemotherapy in glioblastoma, because unmethylated tumors express the repair enzyme that undoes the drug's DNA damage. Make sure you send enough well-preserved tumor, not just necrosis or edematous brain; frozen section helps confirm diagnostic tissue during surgery.

**Hereditary syndromes in neurosurgery**:
- **NF1**: neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas (MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib can shrink them), optic pathway gliomas.
- **NF2-related schwannomatosis**: bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic, plus meningiomas and spinal ependymomas; surgery is timed to balance hearing and facial nerve preservation, and bevacizumab is sometimes used.
- **Von Hippel-Lindau**: cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma; the HIF-2α inhibitor belzutifan now treats VHL-associated tumors.
- **Li-Fraumeni**: avoid unnecessary radiation where possible, because radiation-induced second cancers are a particular risk.
- **Tuberous sclerosis**: subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, which respond to mTOR inhibitors.
- **Lynch syndrome and constitutional mismatch repair deficiency**: some brain tumors with very high mutation burden.

**When to refer for genetics**: young age at diagnosis, multiple primary tumors, characteristic tumor combinations, or family history. Testing changes surveillance for the patient and relatives, and needs genetic counseling.

**Targeted therapy is now in neuro-oncology**: BRAF V600E-mutant gliomas can respond to combined BRAF and MEK inhibitors; vorasidenib targets IDH-mutant low-grade gliomas. Yet the blood-brain barrier and tumor heterogeneity limit many drugs, so surgery and radiation remain central.

keyPoints: Proto-oncogenes promote growth; mutated (gain of function) they become oncogenes, one hit enough
Tumor suppressor genes restrain growth; usually both copies must be lost (Knudson two-hit)
Oncogene activation: point mutation (RAS), amplification (HER2), translocation (BCR-ABL)
TP53 (guardian of the genome) is mutated in about half of cancers
RB controls the G1/S checkpoint; HPV E7 inactivates RB and E6 degrades p53
Inherited mutations explain cancer syndromes (Li-Fraumeni, BRCA, NF1, NF2, VHL)

examples.tr: BCR-ABL fusion oncogene in chronic myeloid leukemia; targeted by imatinib.
One inherited RB mutation plus one somatic hit: early, bilateral tumors.

lessons.title: Hallmarks of Cancer

levels.kid:
Cancer cells are like rule-breakers in a classroom. Scientists made a list of the rules they break.

- They grow even when nobody says 'grow'.
- They ignore the 'stop' signs.
- They refuse to die when they are old or broken.
- They can keep dividing forever.
- They build their own new blood vessels to get food, like sneaking a pipe into the kitchen.
- They push into other places and travel around the body.
- They hide from the body's police, the immune cells.

Scientists call this list the **hallmarks of cancer**. Knowing the rules cancer breaks helps doctors make medicines that stop the rule-breakers.
levels.hs:
In 2000, scientists Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg proposed that all cancers share a set of acquired abilities, the **hallmarks of cancer**. The original six:

1. **Sustaining growth signals**: making their own 'grow' signals or having overactive receptors.
2. **Evading growth suppressors**: ignoring brakes like RB and p53.
3. **Resisting cell death**: avoiding apoptosis, the self-destruct program.
4. **Enabling replicative immortality**: normal cells can divide only a limited number of times because the protective caps on chromosomes, **telomeres**, get shorter with each division. Many cancers turn on **telomerase**, an enzyme that rebuilds them.
5. **Inducing angiogenesis**: growing new blood vessels to bring oxygen and nutrients, using signals like **VEGF**. A tumor cannot grow much beyond a couple of millimeters without its own blood supply.
6. **Activating invasion and metastasis**: breaking loose, invading and spreading.

In 2011 they added more:
- **Reprogramming energy metabolism**: many cancer cells use glucose wastefully even with oxygen available (the **Warburg effect**). This is why PET scans with radioactive glucose make tumors light up.
- **Evading immune destruction**: hiding from immune cells. Immunotherapy drugs remove this disguise.

Two **enabling characteristics** help cancers gain these hallmarks: **genome instability** and **tumor-promoting inflammation**.

Many modern cancer drugs each target one hallmark.
levels.college:
**Sustained proliferative signaling**: autocrine growth factor loops (PDGF in glioma), receptor overexpression or mutation (EGFR, HER2), and constitutive downstream signaling (RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR).

**Evading growth suppressors**: loss of RB (or overactivity of cyclin D/CDK4, or loss of p16 encoded by CDKN2A), loss of p53; also loss of contact inhibition (NF2/merlin, E-cadherin).

**Resisting cell death**: overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 (follicular lymphoma), loss of pro-apoptotic BAX/BAK, loss of p53 sensing. Autophagy can support survival under stress.

**Replicative immortality**: the Hayflick limit and telomere-shortening crisis are bypassed by telomerase activation (TERT promoter mutations, common in glioblastoma, melanoma and bladder cancer) or alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), associated with ATRX loss.

**Angiogenesis**: the 'angiogenic switch' tips the balance of VEGF and inhibitors (thrombospondin-1). Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α, inducing VEGF. Tumor vessels are leaky and disorganized; glioblastoma's microvascular proliferation and necrosis are diagnostic features.

**Invasion and metastasis**: loss of E-cadherin, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), matrix metalloproteinases degrading basement membrane, intravasation, survival in circulation (platelet shielding), extravasation and colonization.

**Metabolic reprogramming (Warburg effect)**: aerobic glycolysis provides biosynthetic intermediates for new cells; FDG-PET exploits increased glucose uptake. Glutamine addiction is common.

**Immune evasion**: loss of MHC class I, PD-L1 expression engaging PD-1 on T cells, immunosuppressive cells (regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells). Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) release the brakes.

**Enabling characteristics**: genomic instability (defective DNA repair, chromosomal instability) and tumor-promoting inflammation.

Targeted therapy examples: EGFR and HER2 inhibitors, CDK4/6 inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax, VEGF antibody bevacizumab, PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors.
levels.phd:
Hanahan's 2022 update proposed further candidate hallmarks and enabling characteristics: **unlocking phenotypic plasticity** (dedifferentiation, blocked differentiation and transdifferentiation, such as lineage switching of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma to small cell carcinoma under targeted therapy), **non-mutational epigenetic reprogramming**, **polymorphic microbiomes** (gut and intratumoral bacteria influencing carcinogenesis and therapy response, for example Fusobacterium in colorectal cancer), and **senescent cells**, which can promote tumors through secreted factors despite being growth-arrested themselves.

The framework is useful but debated. Critics note that the hallmarks describe phenotypes, not mechanisms, and that many also characterize normal processes such as wound healing and embryonic development. A cancer is better conceived as an **ecosystem**: the **tumor microenvironment**, including cancer-associated fibroblasts, endothelial cells, pericytes, immune cells and extracellular matrix, co-evolves with malignant cells and supplies several hallmark capabilities.

The brain illustrates this vividly. Glioma cells form **synapses with neurons**: neuron-to-glioma synapses mediated by AMPA receptors drive tumor growth through depolarization, and neuronal activity releases growth signals such as neuroligin-3. Gliomas also form interconnected networks via long membrane tubes (tumor microtubes) linked by gap junctions, which resist radiation and surgical injury by redistributing calcium and allowing repopulation. This emerging field, **cancer neuroscience**, suggests that seizures and tumor growth may share circuits.

Angiogenesis inhibition in glioblastoma shows the limits of targeting single hallmarks: bevacizumab dramatically reduces enhancement and edema on MRI (partly by restoring barrier tightness, a 'pseudoresponse') without prolonging overall survival in trials, and tumors can shift to infiltrative growth along existing vessels (vessel co-option).

Immune evasion in the brain involves low mutation burden, a T-cell-poor 'cold' microenvironment, immunosuppressive myeloid cells, and corticosteroid use, which help explain why checkpoint inhibitors have mostly failed in glioblastoma despite transforming melanoma treatment, including melanoma brain metastases.
levels.expert:
Every hallmark has turned into a clinical decision somewhere.

**Angiogenesis**: bevacizumab in recurrent glioblastoma improves edema and lets patients reduce steroids, but interpret imaging cautiously, since decreased enhancement may be pseudoresponse while non-enhancing infiltrative tumor progresses on FLAIR sequences. The RANO criteria address this. Anti-angiogenics also impair wound healing and raise bleeding and clotting risks; plan surgery around them.

**Metabolism**: FDG-PET is a staging tool for many body cancers, but the brain's high baseline glucose use makes FDG less useful for brain tumors; amino-acid PET tracers (such as FET or fluciclovine) can better delineate gliomas and distinguish recurrence from treatment effect.

**Immune evasion**: checkpoint inhibitors have transformed metastatic melanoma and lung cancer, including control of some brain metastases, often combined with stereotactic radiosurgery. Their immune-related side effects can involve any organ, including hypophysitis (headache, fatigue, low cortisol), encephalitis, myasthenia-like syndromes and colitis. A patient on immunotherapy with new headache and fatigue needs pituitary hormone testing.

**Corticosteroids are a double-edged tool**: dexamethasone controls tumor edema rapidly but suppresses the immune response that immunotherapies rely on, causes hyperglycemia, myopathy and infection risk, and can obscure the diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma by shrinking it before biopsy. If lymphoma is suspected, avoid steroids before biopsy when the patient is stable.

**Pseudoprogression**: after chemoradiation for glioblastoma, increased enhancement within the first months may be treatment effect rather than tumor growth, more common in MGMT-methylated tumors. Rushing to reoperate or change therapy can harm. Advanced MRI (perfusion, spectroscopy) and time help.

**Tumor treating fields**, alternating electric fields applied to the scalp that disrupt dividing cells, improved survival in a trial for newly diagnosed glioblastoma. A reminder that 'sustaining proliferation' can be attacked by physics as well as chemistry.

keyPoints: Original six hallmarks: growth signals, evading suppressors, resisting death, immortality, angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis
Added: reprogrammed metabolism (Warburg effect) and immune evasion
Enabling characteristics: genome instability and tumor-promoting inflammation
Telomerase rebuilds telomeres, enabling unlimited division
VEGF drives angiogenesis; tumors need vessels to grow beyond a few millimeters
Each hallmark is a target: e.g. bevacizumab (VEGF), checkpoint inhibitors (immune evasion)

examples.tr: Tumors take up more glucose (Warburg effect), so they light up.

lessons.title: Grading, Staging and Tumor Markers

levels.kid:
When doctors find a cancer, they ask two big questions.

First: **How wild do the cells look?** They look under a microscope. Cells that look almost normal get a low number. Cells that look messy and strange get a high number. That number is the **grade**.

Second: **How far has it spread?** Is it still a small spot, or has it moved to other places? That is the **stage**. Think of a spilled drink: a tiny drop on the table is easy to clean, but a spill that ran across the floor is harder.

Some cancers also leave clues in the blood, like footprints. Doctors call those clues **tumor markers**.

Knowing the grade and stage helps doctors choose the best plan.
levels.hs:
Once a cancer is diagnosed, doctors describe it in two ways.

**Grade** describes how abnormal the cancer cells look under a microscope, and how fast they seem to be dividing.
- **Low grade** (well differentiated): cells resemble normal tissue; usually slower growing.
- **High grade** (poorly differentiated or anaplastic): cells look very abnormal; usually faster growing.

**Stage** describes how far the cancer has spread in the body. For most solid tumors, doctors use the **TNM system**:
- **T** = size and extent of the primary **tumor**.
- **N** = spread to nearby lymph **nodes**.
- **M** = **metastasis** to distant sites (M0 = none, M1 = present).
These combine into an overall stage from I (early, localized) to IV (distant spread).

For most cancers, **stage predicts outcome better than grade**. Doctors determine stage with physical exams, imaging (CT, MRI, PET), biopsies and surgery.

**Tumor markers** are substances made by tumors (or by the body in response) that can be measured in blood. Examples:
- **PSA**: prostate cancer.
- **CEA**: colorectal cancer.
- **AFP**: liver cancer and some testicular cancers.
- **hCG**: certain testicular and placental tumors.
- **CA-125**: ovarian cancer.

Tumor markers are mostly useful for **monitoring treatment and checking for recurrence**, not for diagnosing cancer on their own, because they can be raised in harmless conditions too.
levels.college:
**Grading** systems are tumor-specific:
- **Gleason score** and the newer **Grade Groups** (1-5) in prostate cancer, based on glandular architecture.
- **Nottingham grade** in breast cancer: tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic count.
- **WHO CNS grades 1-4**, assigned within tumor types and integrating molecular features since 2021.
- Proliferation index **Ki-67** supports grading in neuroendocrine tumors and others.

**Staging** uses the AJCC/UICC **TNM** classification. Prefixes matter: c (clinical), p (pathologic, after surgery), y (after neoadjuvant therapy), r (recurrence). Lymphomas use the **Lugano (Ann Arbor-based)** system; most primary brain tumors are not TNM staged, because they rarely metastasize outside the CNS, and grade, molecular markers, extent of resection and patient factors drive prognosis instead.

**Prognostic factors** beyond stage and grade: performance status (ECOG or Karnofsky), age, molecular features (HER2, hormone receptors, EGFR, ALK, MGMT, IDH), lymphovascular invasion and margin status.

**Tumor markers**:
- **PSA**: prostate cancer; also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis.
- **CEA**: colorectal cancer monitoring; raised in smokers and inflammatory conditions.
- **AFP**: hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumors; normally high in fetuses.
- **β-hCG**: choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic disease, some germ cell tumors.
- **CA-125**: epithelial ovarian cancer; also endometriosis, peritoneal irritation.
- **CA 19-9**: pancreatic cancer.
- **Calcitonin**: medullary thyroid carcinoma.
- **LDH**: nonspecific marker of tumor burden (lymphoma, germ cell tumors, melanoma).

Markers have low positive predictive value in screening populations; their main roles are monitoring response and detecting relapse, and in specific contexts contributing to diagnosis (AFP with characteristic imaging in cirrhosis; AFP and β-hCG in germ cell tumors).

**Screening** principles: a test must detect disease early enough to change outcome, with acceptable harms, overdiagnosis and cost. Lead-time bias and length-time bias can make screening look better than it is.
levels.phd:
Staging systems are evolving from anatomy toward **biology**. The eighth edition of the AJCC manual incorporated biomarkers into breast cancer staging (grade, hormone receptor and HER2 status, and multigene recurrence scores can shift the prognostic stage), and HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer received its own staging because it carries a far better prognosis than HPV-negative disease at the same anatomic extent. Anatomic TNM remains essential for comparing populations, but individual prognosis increasingly depends on molecular class.

**Liquid biopsy** is transforming tumor markers. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), detected by sequencing tumor-specific mutations or methylation patterns in plasma cell-free DNA, can detect **minimal residual disease** after surgery, predict relapse months before imaging, and track resistance mutations during targeted therapy (for example EGFR T790M). Multi-cancer early detection tests based on methylation patterns are under evaluation, with open questions about sensitivity for early-stage tumors, false positives, overdiagnosis and mortality benefit, which has not yet been shown.

The brain poses special challenges: ctDNA from brain tumors is scarce in plasma because of the blood-brain barrier, but **CSF ctDNA** detects tumor mutations more reliably and can aid diagnosis of tumors in risky locations, such as diffuse midline glioma with H3 K27M.

**DNA methylation profiling** has become a powerful classifier for CNS tumors: a reference classifier built from thousands of tumors assigns methylation classes that sometimes change the histologic diagnosis, and methylation classes stratify meningioma recurrence risk better than WHO grade alone. Integrated grading schemes for meningioma now combine histology, CDKN2A/B deletion and TERT promoter mutation (which define grade 3), and copy number features.

Statistical pitfalls haunt staging research: **stage migration** (the 'Will Rogers phenomenon') occurs when better imaging moves patients with small metastases from a lower stage into a higher one, improving the survival of both groups without any patient living longer.
levels.expert:
Clinicians stage before they treat, and the staging workup should match the cancer: chest, abdomen and pelvis CT for most solid tumors, PET-CT for lung cancer and lymphoma, brain MRI when the primary frequently goes to the brain (lung cancer, melanoma, HER2-positive or triple-negative breast cancer).

**Multidisciplinary tumor boards** turn stage, grade and molecular data into a plan: surgery, radiation, systemic therapy, or surveillance. Neurosurgeons sit on neuro-oncology and spine boards.

**Germ cell tumors of the brain** show tumor markers at their most powerful. In a pineal or suprasellar mass in a young patient, serum and CSF AFP and β-hCG are measured before surgery. Clearly raised markers can establish a non-germinomatous germ cell tumor and lead straight to chemotherapy without biopsy; a pure germinoma is highly radio- and chemosensitive. Obstructive hydrocephalus is often handled first with endoscopic third ventriculostomy, which can include biopsy and CSF sampling in the same procedure.

**Pituitary tumors**: a prolactin level is essential before operating on a sellar mass, because prolactinomas usually respond to dopamine agonists and do not need surgery. Beware the 'hook effect': a huge prolactinoma can give a falsely modest prolactin result unless the sample is diluted. A modest prolactin elevation with a large non-secreting adenoma usually reflects stalk compression.

**Spinal metastases**: decisions use frameworks such as **NOMS** (neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, systemic). Epidural spinal cord compression grade, radiosensitivity of the tumor, mechanical instability (the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score) and overall prognosis decide between radiation, stereotactic radiosurgery, separation surgery plus radiosurgery, or stabilization. A landmark trial showed that surgery plus radiation helped selected patients with cord compression walk again more than radiation alone.

**Performance status** often matters as much as stage: a patient with Karnofsky below about 70 or ECOG 3-4 may be harmed rather than helped by aggressive treatment. Goals of care belong in every staging conversation.

keyPoints: Grade = how abnormal cells look (differentiation, mitoses); stage = how far the cancer has spread
TNM: T tumor size/extent, N nodes, M metastasis; stages I-IV
For most cancers, stage predicts outcome better than grade
Tumor markers (PSA, CEA, AFP, β-hCG, CA-125, CA 19-9) mainly monitor response and recurrence
Markers are not specific enough for diagnosis or screening alone
Brain tumors use WHO grades 1-4 with molecular features, not TNM
